title: Sequence, background and time

objectives.can: Tell the main line of a narrative from its background: wayyiqtol chains broken by וְ + subject + qatal, participles and verbless clauses; and read וַיְהִי with a time expression.

explanation.summary: A Hebrew story has a main line of events and, alongside it, clauses that give the setting, the reasons and what was going on. The verb form and the word order tell you which is which. Once you can sort them, a chapter of narrative stops being a flat string of 'and's.

sections.heading: The main line and what stands off it
body: In the last lesson you met the wayyiqtol chain. In narrative it usually carries the main line: one event after another, each clause starting with a verb. That is the account given by modern discourse grammar, and it is widely, though not universally, shared among scholars. Use it as a working rule and watch for the places where it does not seem to fit.

Clauses that step aside from the main line give something else: the circumstances in which an event happened, an event that happened earlier, a contrast, an explanation, a description of a person or a place. They are not the next event. Hebrew marks them mainly by what comes first in the clause. When the clause begins with וְ and something other than a verb, the chain is broken, and the clause that follows is usually background.

sections.heading: Four signs of a clause off the line
body: The table lists the common kinds, each with an example from the passages of this lesson. The last column states a tendency, not a rule, and the context has the last word.

head: Clause type
Example
What it tends to do
rows: the next event on the main line
an earlier or simultaneous event, a contrast or a new scene
what was going on, a state in progress
a description of a person or a place
what a character sees, shown from his or her point of view

sections.heading: Reading the signs
body: A qatal that follows וְ and a noun or pronoun is the commonest sign. The subject is put first because the writer is not telling the next event. In Ruth 1:22 the clause וְהֵמָּה בָּאוּ adds that the two women had come at a particular time of year. In Genesis 22:1 the clause וְהָאֱלֹהִים נִסָּה gives the reader something Abraham does not know: that God is testing him.

A qatal in a clause with כִּי, 'for', often gives a reason that lies behind the main line, as when Naomi rises 'for she had heard' that the Lord had visited his people. A participle presents an action as going on while the story proceeds, as when Eli is described sitting by the door of the temple. A verbless clause describes: of Hannah, וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ, 'and she was bitter of soul'.
Then the main line picks up again with a wayyiqtol. This is the signal that the background is over: וַתִּתְפַּלֵּל, 'and she prayed', takes the story on from the description.

sections.heading: Marking time: וַיְהִי with a time expression
body: A story often begins a new section with וַיְהִי followed by a phrase that says when: וַיְהִי אַחֲרֵי הַדְּבָרִים הָאֵלֶּה, 'and it happened after these things'. Another form joins the verb to a preposition and an infinitive, as in Ruth 1:19, וַיְהִי כְּבֹאָנָה בֵּית לֶחֶם, 'and it happened when they came to Bethlehem'. In both cases the וַיְהִי gives the time, and the event that matters follows in a second verb: in Genesis 22:20 וַיֻּגַּד, 'it was told', and in Ruth 1:19 וַתֵּהֹם, 'was stirred'.
Not every time expression needs a וַיְהִי. A phrase may simply stand first in the clause, as in Genesis 22:4, 'on the third day', and the wayyiqtol that follows carries on.

misunderstandings: A qatal in a narrative is not an error for a wayyiqtol. It is the writer's way of saying that the clause is not the next event. The reader has to ask what it is: an earlier event, a reason, a contrast or a state.
Background does not mean unimportant. The sentence about God testing Abraham is background to the action of the scene and is also the most important thing the reader is told.

וַיְהִי does not always carry a time phrase and it is not always translated. It can introduce a character or a state ('there was a man'), and it can open a scene with a time phrase. English 'it happened' is only one way to render it.
These rules describe tendencies of narrative. Scholars differ about particular verses, and the analysed text does not decide them for you.

deeper.heading: How firm is the main-line rule?
body: Discourse grammar is a modern way of describing patterns that the older grammars treated under 'waw consecutive' and 'circumstantial clauses'. The older grammars list the same clause types, but explain them differently. For reading, the practical point is the same: a clause that does not begin with a wayyiqtol is likely to be doing something other than moving the story one step on.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: So Naomi returned, and Ruth the Moabitess, her daughter-in-law, with her, who returned out of the field of Moab — and they came to Beth-lehem in the beginning of barley harvest.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The verse ends the chapter. וַתָּשָׁב is the wayyiqtol: Naomi returned. The next clause begins with וְהֵמָּה, a pronoun, before the qatal בָּאוּ. It does not give a new event but says when they arrived, at the beginning of the barley harvest. That is background that prepares for the next chapter.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And Abraham lifted up his eyes, and looked, and behold behind him a ram caught in the thicket by his horns. And Abraham went and took the ram, and offered him up for a burnt-offering in the stead of his son.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A chain of wayyiqtols (he lifted, he saw), and then וְהִנֵּה, 'and look!', which presents what Abraham sees: a ram. Its description, with the qatal נֶאֱחַז, 'caught', belongs inside what he sees. Then the wayyiqtols resume: he went, he took.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: Now Hannah, she spoke in her heart; only her lips moved, but her voice could not be heard; therefore, Eli thought she had been drunken.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: The clauses begin with וְחַנָּה, a noun, and are not on the main line. מְדַבֶּרֶת is a participle: Hannah was speaking in her heart. Another participle, נָּעוֹת, adds that her lips were moving. The yiqtol יִשָּׁמֵעַ describes her voice. Then the chain resumes with the wayyiqtol וַיַּחְשְׁבֶהָ: Eli thought she was drunk. We see the scene as Eli does.

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: So they two went until they came to Beth-lehem. And it came to pass, when they were come to Beth-lehem, that all the city was astir concerning them, and the women said: 'Is this Naomi?'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: A wayyiqtol takes the two women to Bethlehem. Then וַיְהִי with כְּבֹאָנָה, 'when they came', gives the time. The event the verse is about follows: the whole town was stirred (וַתֵּהֹם), and the women said (וַתֹּאמַרְנָה) whether this was Naomi.

quoted.title: Genesis
quoted.english: And it came to pass after these things, that God did prove Abraham, and said unto him: 'Abraham'; and he said: 'Here am I.'
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

examples.analysis: וַיְהִי with a time phrase opens the episode. The reader is then told, in a clause that begins with the subject, that God tested Abraham (נִסָּה, a qatal). It is background for the scene. The speaking begins with the wayyiqtol וַיֹּאמֶר.

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: So Hannah rose up after they had eaten in Shiloh, and after they had drunk — now Eli the priest sat upon his seat by the door-post of the temple of the LORD;
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is a command to Hannah
It describes the setting: Eli was sitting there, which belongs to the background
It reports the next event: Eli sat down
practice.explain: The clause begins with the subject and has a participle, not a wayyiqtol. It says what Eli was doing, and the story then returns to Hannah.

practice.prompt: The clause וְהִיא מָרַת נָפֶשׁ (words 0–2) has no verb. What does it give, and which word then continues the main line?

options: An event; וְהִיא (word 0) takes the story on
A question; מָרַת (word 1) takes the story on
A description of how Hannah felt; וַתִּתְפַּלֵּל (word 3) takes the story on
practice.explain: A verbless clause describes a state. The wayyiqtol that follows returns to the events: she prayed.

quoted.english: And she went forth out of the place where she was, and her two daughters-in-law with her; and they went on the way to return unto the land of Judah.

options: הָיְתָה (word 4), because it is a verb of being
practice.explain: The two wayyiqtols are what Naomi does: she went out and they walked. הָיְתָה sits in a relative clause, 'the place where she was', which only identifies the place.

quoted.english: And it came to pass after these things, that it was told Abraham, saying: 'Behold, Milcah, she also hath borne children unto thy brother Nahor:

options: It begins a command; the speech follows
It reports an event inside the earlier scene
It sets a new time after the earlier events and opens a new section; the wayyiqtol וַיֻּגַּד (word 4) gives the first event
practice.explain: וַיְהִי with a time phrase is a common way to open a new section. The event itself, the news brought to Abraham, comes in the next verb.

options: It turns the verb into a future
It places the next event in time, while the wayyiqtol keeps the story moving
It makes the clause a question
It stops the story and begins background
practice.explain: The phrase is a time adverb at the head of the clause. The verb is still a wayyiqtol, and the chain goes on.

check.prompt: What does the first וַיְהִי (word 0), with בִּימֵי (word 1), do in the opening of the book?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: AND IT came to pass in the days when the judges judged, that there was a famine in the land. And a certain man of Beth-lehem in Judah went to sojourn in the field of Moab, he, and his wife, and his two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It commands the reader to be in the days of the judges
It names the time when the story takes place, and a second וַיְהִי (word 4) brings in the famine
check.explain: The first וַיְהִי with the time phrase sets the setting, 'in the days when the judges judged'. The second וַיְהִי introduces the circumstance, a famine, and the first action follows with וַיֵּלֶךְ.

check.prompt: How do the yiqtol יַעֲשֶׂה (word 1) and the wayyiqtol וַתִּבְכֶּה (word 10) differ in what they do?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: And as he did so year by year, when she went up to the house of the LORD, so she vexed her; therefore she wept, and would not eat.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: Both are descriptions of the future
The yiqtol is a command and the wayyiqtol is a wish
The yiqtol describes what he did every year; the wayyiqtol tells Hannah's response, taking the story on
check.explain: 'Year by year' shows that the yiqtol describes a repeated situation. The wayyiqtol then moves on to what Hannah did, and the chain continues.

check.prompt: Verse 2 begins with verbless clauses that give names. Which word resumes the main line?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And the name of the man was Elimelech, and the name of his wife Naomi, and the name of his two sons Mahlon and Chilion, Ephrathites of Beth-lehem in Judah. And they came into the field of Moab, and continued there.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

check.explain: The names are description. The first wayyiqtol, וַיָּבֹאוּ, 'and they came', brings the family to Moab and carries the story on.

check.prompt: What does וַיְהִי (word 0) do before אִישׁ אֶחָד (words 1–2) at the head of the book?

quoted.title: 1 Samuel
quoted.english: NOW THERE was a certain man of Ramathaim-zophim, of the hill-country of Ephraim, and his name was Elkanah, the son of Jeroham, the son of Elihu, the son of Tohu, the son of Zuph, an Ephraimite.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It introduces a character: 'there was a certain man'
It reports a past event of the man's travels
It marks a time: 'when the man came'
check.explain: Here וַיְהִי simply states that someone existed, and the rest of the verse describes him with his family line. It is not a time clause.

check.prompt: How does וַתִּשָּׁאֵר (word 4) relate to וַיָּמָת (word 0)?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And Elimelech Naomi's husband died; and she was left, and her two sons.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: It is background to the death
It is the next event on the main line: Elimelech died and Naomi was left
check.explain: Both are wayyiqtols, so both are on the main line. The second follows from the first.

check.prompt: After the wayyiqtols about Orpah, the clause וְרוּת דָּבְקָה בָּהּ (words 7–9) puts the subject before the qatal. What does this word order suggest?

quoted.title: Ruth
quoted.english: And they lifted up their voice, and wept again; and Orpah kissed her mother-in-law; but Ruth cleaved unto her.
quoted.credit: Open Scriptures Hebrew Bible (OSHB), morphology and lemmas by the OSHB project; text: Westminster Leningrad Codex (WLC)

options: A contrast: Orpah kissed her mother-in-law, but Ruth held on
check.explain: The subject comes first and the verb is a qatal, so the clause is not the next step of a chain. Many readers take it as a contrast with what Orpah does.

reading.why: Five verses in which the main line (she rose, she prayed, Eli thought) alternates with participle clauses and verbless clauses that show the scene through Eli's eyes: the best passage in the lesson for sorting foreground from background.
